# Strategies for Transitioning Residents to Digital Payments


November 02, 2026


by Emma Lunceford


##


Government organizations are increasingly focused on helping residents embrace and transition to digital payments. Morgan Jines, vice president of payments, recently shared practical strategies for increasing adoption and driving online transactions.


According to Jines, government organizations have made significant strides in digital payments, but providing a payment solution doesn’t guarantee residents will use it. Driving increased digital adoption requires a strategic plan to meet residents where they are and encourage them to change payment behavior.


## The Awareness Challenge


One of the most important factors hindering adoption is awareness. “Awareness is often one of the biggest barriers. It generally rises to the top,” Jines noted. Are residents informed about the available solutions? Have agencies reached residents effectively at every possible touchpoint?


Building awareness and boosting visibility is not a one-time effort; it requires a sustained communication strategy. Governments should utilize materials that appeal to all generations, ensuring residents are consistently reminded of digital payment options. Establishing clear, measurable goals is also vital for tracking progress and refining tactics. For example, one county in Missouri set specific objectives and promoted new payment channels through flyers and updated website messaging. Their efforts included in-office flyers to capture foot traffic and broader online announcements. As a result, the county saw a 23% increase in payment adoption within five months.


## Meeting Residents Where They Are


To drive successful adoption, agencies must prioritize both awareness and user experience. Simply informing residents about a digital payment option is not enough —adoption depends on whether the solution genuinely enhances their experience. Residents now expect seamless, consumer-grade payment processes like those found in retail. Providing a variety of payment options, such as online, mobile, digital wallets, text-to-pay, and IVR, ensures agencies can accommodate different preferences and lifestyles. As Jines shared, “Adoption rises when governments meet residents where and how they want to pay.” This, in turn, reduces friction and encourages residents to adopt new solutions. Jines shared that a Colorado city sought to increase autopay enrollment by giving residents the option to add a card to their account and avoid missing a payment. After the campaign, the city found that by offering seamless payment options and promoting them effectively, they achieved 3,775 autopay enrollments, a 19% increase overall.


## Adoption is an Ongoing Program


An important consideration is that adoption efforts don’t end when a campaign ends. Adoption requires continual effort to maintain momentum, engage residents, and retool metrics. Resident expectations will continue to rise; payment technology will continue to evolve, and without an ongoing adoption effort, agencies will lose their momentum and the opportunity to create sustained behavior change.


To continue momentum and drive meaningful change, agencies should see digital adoption as an ongoing cycle of assessment, activation, and optimization. A practical approach, Jines said, is to follow a 30/60/90-day roadmap: begin with a 30-day assessment of barriers, baseline metrics, payment options, and adoption goals to establish a starting point. The following 30 days focus on activation through targeted campaigns, staff training, and promotion of specific payment methods, using early data to refine strategies and maximize resident engagement. In the optimization phase, agencies analyze results, address sources of friction, and adjust tactics for continual improvement. This structured, cyclical approach enables agencies to adapt to evolving resident needs, boost digital payment transition, and achieve better long-term outcomes.
